parts: Lesson 21: Spread of Indian Culture Abroad — Summary

India had commercial contact with the outside world from about the middle of the third millennium BC. The most remarkable aspect of the spread of Indian culture and civilisation in Central Asia, South East Asia, China, Japan and Korea is that it was not by conquest or threat but by voluntary acceptance of India's cultural and spiritual values. Traders, teachers, emissaries and missionaries carried it. Traders went to Rome in the west and China in the east and from the 1st century BC to Indonesia and Cambodia in search of gold (Java, Sumatra, Malaya were called Suvarnadvipa) from cities like Kashi, Mathura, Ujjain, Prayag and Pataliputra and ports like Mamallapuram, Tamralipti, Puri and Kaveripattinam; Kalinga traded with Sri Lanka under Ashoka; they served as cultural ambassadors. Buddhist monastic centres on the west coast: Karle, Bhaja, Kanheri, Ajanta and Ellora.

Universities attracted students and scholars: Nalanda (its library a seven-storey building), Valabhi (Hiuen Tsang stayed at both), Vikramashila on the right bank of the Ganga (described by the Tibetan scholar Taranatha; the Tibetan king invited its head), Odantapuri in Bihar (under the Palas; many monks settled in Tibet). Two Indian teachers, Kashyapa Matanga and Dharmarakshita, went to China in AD 67 on the invitation of Emperor Ming Ti; Kumarajiva (5th century) was asked to translate Sanskrit texts into Chinese; Bodhidharma (from Kanchipuram, studied at Nalanda) carried yoga and dhyana (ch'an), worshipped in China and Japan; Acharya Kamalashila of Nalanda was invited by the king of Tibet (his body was embalmed in a Lhasa monastery); Jnanabhadra went to Tibet with his sons; Acharya Atisha (Dipankara Shrijnana), head of Vikramashila, went to Tibet in the 11th century; Thonmi Sambhota, a Tibetan minister, studied at Nalanda and preached Buddhism; the king declared Buddhism the state religion. Romas or Gypsies went west as wanderers through Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran, Iraq and Turkey over about 400 years, keeping their language Romani, customs, professions, dance and music.

From the 2nd century BC India had contact with China, Central Asia, West Asia and Rome; the route used by traders to China became the Silk Route because silk was a chief commodity; later monks and scholars used it; Buddhism was the most lasting treasure carried. Kuchi was a flourishing centre of Indian culture where the Silk Route divided into northern (Samarkand, Kashgar, Turfan, Hami) and southern (Yarkand, Khotan, Miran) routes meeting at the Dunhuang caves. Khotan, on the southern route, was famous for silk, dance, music and gold and jade; its first-century coins had Chinese on one side and Prakrit in Kharoshthi on the other; Sanskrit manuscripts were found in monasteries buried in sand. China: contact from the 2nd century BC; Emperor Ming Ti (AD 67) invited the monks; Chinese pilgrims' accounts are important sources of Indian history; Buddhist philosophy appealed to intellectuals who had Confucianism; the Wei dynasty's first emperor declared Buddhism the state religion in the 4th century; thousands of Sanskrit books were translated; cave temples at Dunhuang, Yungang and Longmen show Indian influence. Korea received Indian culture through China: the monk Sundo, the first Buddhist monk to enter Korea (AD 352) with a Buddha image and sutras; Acharya Maranananda (AD 384); an Indian monk built two temples at Pyongyang (AD 404); dhyana yoga reached Korea in the 8th–9th century; Buddhist texts were printed in 6000 volumes. Japan: earliest evidence AD 552 when the Korean emperor sent a Buddha statue, sutras, artists, sculptors, painters and architects; Buddhism became the state religion; Sanskrit was accepted as a sacred language, and its syllables and mantras were written in the Shittan (Siddham) script; Prince Shotoku (7th century) was impressed by Buddhist sutras. Tibet: king Naradeva (Srong-tsan-gampo) sent minister Thonmi Sambhota with sixteen scholars to Magadha; he devised the Tibetan script from Brahmi in the 7th century (it influenced the scripts of Mongolia and Manchuria) and wrote a grammar based on Panini; ninety-six thousand Sanskrit books were translated into Tibetan between the 7th and 17th centuries.

Sri Lanka: Ashoka sent his son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra with a cutting of the Bodhi tree to King Devanampiya Tissa; the first monasteries were Mahavihara and Abhayagiri; Pali became the literary language; Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa are Buddhist chronicles; Sigiriya cave-shelter monasteries have paintings in the Amaravati style (King Kashyapa fortified it in the 5th century). Myanmar: Indians from Amaravati and Tamralipti settled after the 2nd century AD; Pagan (11th–13th century) with Shwezigon pagoda built by King Anawrahta (Aniruddha); Brahmin ponnas were court astrologers. Thailand (Siam till 1939): influences from the 1st century AD; Sanskrit names for kingdoms (Dvaravati, Srivijaya, Sukhodaya, Ayutthaya) and cities (Kanchanaburi, Lopburi from Lavapuri); earliest images are of Vishnu; Ayutthaya (Ayodhya); 400 temples in Bangkok. Cambodia (Kambuja): Kaundinya dynasty from the 1st century; Sanskrit inscriptions; Sanskrit as administrative language till the 14th century; kings with Sanskrit names; Hindu polity and Brahmin jurisprudence; Indian month names; Angkor Vat – abode of Vishnu (Vaikuntha), five towers as the five peaks of Mount Sumeru, king Suryavarman as an incarnation of Vishnu, square mile of construction with a moat, scenes of the Ramayana and Mahabharata, the largest scene being the Samudra Manthan; Baphuon temple at Yashodharapura (11th century) with the Rama–Ravana battle, Shiva on Kailasa and the destruction of Kamadeva. Vietnam (Champa): cities named Indrapura, Amaravati, Vijaya, Kauthara and Panduranga; the people are called Cham; they worshipped Shiva, Ganesha, Saraswati, Lakshmi, Parvati, Buddha and Lokeshwara. Malaysia: Shaivism in Kedah and Wellesley; Nandi head, Durga relief, Ganesha and Shivalingas of the 7th–8th centuries; late Brahmi script; Sanskrit words (svarga, rasa, guna, mantri, laksha); Ligor inscription and over fifty temples. Indonesia: Prambanan, the largest Shiva temple in Java (9th century) flanked by Vishnu and Brahma temples, with vahana temples for Nandi, Garuda and the goose, Durga and Ganesha temples, eight big temples surrounded by 240 small ones; Ramayana and Krishna stories carved; Bali still follows Hindu culture and has over five hundred Sanskrit hymns; Kawi script based on Brahmi; Bhuvanakosha text with 525 Sanskrit shlokas; the Wayang shadow play of the epics. Varna was known but less rigid.

Arab accounts (Sulaiman the merchant, Al-Masudi, Ibn Hauqal, Al-Idrisi) from the mid-9th century show flourishing trade; cultural contact goes back to the 8th century: the Brahmasphutasiddhanta (Sindhind) and Khandakhadyaka (Arkand) were taken to Baghdad and translated by Alfazari; works of Aryabhata and Varahamihira were studied; mathematics was called 'hindisa'; the Arabs appreciated the decimal system with zero; at Caliph Harun al-Rashid's behest (AD 786–809) Indian medical works were translated (Sushruta Samhita by Mankh); they also studied snake poison, veterinary art, logic, philosophy, ethics, politics and warfare; Arabic words for shipping have Indian origins. Rome: in the first three centuries AD South India had a profitable sea trade with the Roman Empire, India's best customer (Roman coins found at Coimbatore and Madurai; exports pepper, betel, spices, scents, beryl, diamonds, pearls, ivory, silk, muslin) which brought gold and a stable gold currency for the Kushana empire; yavanas (Greeks and Romans) guarded Tamil kings' tents and Madurai's gates; Kaveripattinam's warehouses stamped with the Chola tiger emblem; Pliny deplored the drain of gold; ports at Sopara and Barygaza (Broach); Chola lighthouses; Arretine pottery at Arikamedu near Pondicherry; Andhra king Yajnasri issued coins with a ship. Samudragupta had a strong navy; the Cholas raided across the sea. What Indians learnt: minting of gold coins from Greece and Rome, silk-making from China, betel-growing from Indonesia.
